Industrial Subsidies and Trade Realignment: Analyzing the IRA and EU Chips Act

Author: Pierre Dupont | December 2, 2025 | Trade Policy Division

Subsidies as Catalysts for Industrial Relocation

The re-emergence of targeted industrial policy has triggered an unprecedented competition in state capital subsidies across North America and Europe. Under the United States Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the CHIPS and Science Act, over $430 billion in direct tax credits, manufacturing incentives, and loan guarantees have been earmarked for domestic clean tech, battery, and semiconductor production.

In response, the European Union established the European Chips Act, mobilizing 43 billion euros in public and private investments, coupled with the Net-Zero Industry Act to prevent capital flight across the Atlantic. Cross-border greenfield foreign direct investment (FDI) into US and European clean manufacturing jumped 64% year-over-year between 2023 and 2025.

Distortionary Spillover Effects on Allied Trading Partners

While friend-shoring initiatives aim to bolster resilience among allied democratic nations, unilateral domestic local-content requirements have created diplomatic and commercial tensions among OECD allies. Automotive manufacturers in Japan, South Korea, and Germany initially faced exclusion from consumer EV tax credits, prompting rapid bilateral negotiations and memorandum of understanding (MoU) frameworks regarding critical mineral sourcing.

Subsidized capital deployment risks creating regional production overcapacity in certain battery cell components, with global lithium-ion manufacturing capacity projected to exceed actual automotive demand by 2.4 times by 2028.
